items.label: f02-adoption-modes
items.front: authAdoptionMode(current, next) in src/lib/sync.ts:14-20 returns guest, same-account or account-switch. What does the provider do for guest vs account-switch?
items.back: guest (current null): no wipe - guest outbox events are kept and synced under the new account. account-switch (a to b): wipe A's baseline and outbox before adopting B, so one account's events never sync as another's.

items.label: f03-review-criteria
items.front: Review criteria for sync changes (atomic commit at src/lib/storage.ts:42-52): list the five conditions.
items.back: setSession invalidation before clearing account data; baseline write and ack deletion in one transaction; acks limited to the sent batch; publication re-reads storage; and each has a test that fails when the line is removed.

items.label: f01-ownership-principle
items.front: State the single ownership principle behind the generation checks, the adoption/logout ordering and applyUserUpdate (see runOnce, src/lib/sync.ts:79-82).
items.back: Asynchronous results may mutate local account state only while their issuing session remains active. Each request captures its generation; every commit point re-checks it, and logout/adoption invalidate old work (setSession) before replacing account data.

items.label: f04-swallowed-failures
items.front: Finding F4: syncNow ends in .catch(() => {}) (src/lib/progress.tsx:87). What is the operational cost?
items.back: Nothing records why a sync failed. The only signal is pendingCount not decreasing, so auth, network and server failures are indistinguishable and invisible.

items.prompt: Deleting the generation half of the guard on sync.ts line 99 leaves all six coordinator tests green. Why?

choices.text: No test re-logs in as the same user; user-id checks catch the other cases
The tests mock the coordinator itself, so line 99 is not actually executed
Vitest skips assertions placed inside async callbacks unless told otherwise
The generation check on line 80 already makes the one on line 99 redundant

choices: No test re-logs in as the same user; user-id checks catch the other cases
The tests mock the coordinator itself, so line 99 is not actually executed
Vitest skips assertions placed inside async callbacks unless told otherwise
The generation check on line 80 already makes the one on line 99 redundant

items.explanation: The tests only switch to a different user or to logged out, which the user-id half already catches. The case that needs the generation is described but untested; exercise 6's same-user test kills the mutation.

items.prompt: Why does onCommit receive a fresh readOutbox() instead of the array read before the request?

choices.text: Because push mutated the pre-request array in place, so it is no longer valid
Because calling readOutbox is cheaper than copying the old array
Because React needs a new array reference before it will re-render
Events recorded while the request was pending must stay visible after commit

choices: Because push mutated the pre-request array in place, so it is no longer valid
Because calling readOutbox is cheaper than copying the old array
Because React needs a new array reference before it will re-render
Events recorded while the request was pending must stay visible after commit

items.explanation: Publishing the pre-request array would re-show acknowledged events or hide new ones. Publication re-reads storage after the commit so the displayed state matches what is actually queued.

items.prompt: The server's /sync response lists some events as rejected. What does the app do with them?

choices.text: They are shown to the user in a sync error banner on the progress home screen
They are acknowledged like the rest, so they leave the outbox unreported
They stay in the outbox and are retried again on each later sync
They are moved to a separate dead-letter table for later review

choices: They are shown to the user in a sync error banner on the progress home screen
They are acknowledged like the rest, so they leave the outbox unreported
They stay in the outbox and are retried again on each later sync
They are moved to a separate dead-letter table for later review

items.explanation: The push adapter acknowledges every sent id and ignores rejected, so those events are deleted from the outbox and never surfaced or logged. Deleting poison rows may be fine, but it should be a visible decision rather than a silent side effect.

items.prompt: A sync request is pending when the user logs out and signs back into the SAME account. Why is a user-id check alone not enough to discard the old response?

choices.text: Because access tokens are compared instead of ids, and those are identical
It is enough on its own - the server rejects requests from earlier sessions
Because the user id changes on each login, so the check would always fail
The id matches again; only the generation, bumped per setSession, differs

choices: Because access tokens are compared instead of ids, and those are identical
It is enough on its own - the server rejects requests from earlier sessions
Because the user id changes on each login, so the check would always fail
The id matches again; only the generation, bumped per setSession, differs

items.explanation: The user id matches again, but the request belongs to an abandoned session. The coordinator increments generation on every setSession and captures it when sync is requested, so a same-identity re-login still invalidates old work.

items.prompt: What replaced the original separate baseline write followed by outboxClear?

choices.text: The same two writes, reordered so the outbox is cleared before the baseline
commitSyncedProgress: upsert baseline and delete acked ids in one transaction
A server-side endpoint that clears the device's outbox remotely after sync
An in-memory cache that is flushed to SQLite when the app is backgrounded

choices: The same two writes, reordered so the outbox is cleared before the baseline
commitSyncedProgress: upsert baseline and delete acked ids in one transaction
A server-side endpoint that clears the device's outbox remotely after sync
An in-memory cache that is flushed to SQLite when the app is backgrounded

items.explanation: commitSyncedProgress upserts the baseline and deletes only the acknowledged ids inside one SQLite transaction. Writing baseline and deleting acknowledgements together means a crash cannot leave one without the other.

items.prompt: push returns acknowledgedIds ["a", "c"] but only event a was in the sent batch; c was recorded while the request was pending. What gets deleted from the outbox?

choices.text: Both a and c, because the server acknowledged both of those ids
Neither - an ack for an id outside the batch aborts the commit
The whole outbox, since the server returned fresh progress state
Only a - acks are intersected with the sent batch, so c stays queued

choices: Both a and c, because the server acknowledged both of those ids
Neither - an ack for an id outside the batch aborts the commit
The whole outbox, since the server returned fresh progress state
Only a - acks are intersected with the sent batch, so c stays queued

items.explanation: The acknowledgement boundary is narrower than clearing the outbox: only identifiers present in the sent batch may be removed.

items.prompt: push rejects with a network error that has no status. What happens?

choices.text: A refresh is attempted for this failure too, and then push retries once
The coordinator retries the push itself with exponential backoff
It is rethrown; only a 401 triggers a refresh, and nothing is committed
The batch is acknowledged anyway, so the outbox does not grow forever

choices: A refresh is attempted for this failure too, and then push retries once
The coordinator retries the push itself with exponential backoff
It is rethrown; only a 401 triggers a refresh, and nothing is committed
The batch is acknowledged anyway, so the outbox does not grow forever

items.explanation: Only a 401 triggers a refresh, and nothing is committed or acknowledged. Other failures propagate without pretending progress was committed.

items.prompt: sync() stores this.tail = operation.catch(() => undefined) but returns operation itself. What would break if it stored this.tail = operation?

choices.text: The caller would stop receiving rejections from syncs that had failed
Concurrent syncs would start running in parallel instead of one at a time
After one failure, each later sync() chains onto a rejection and never runs
Nothing important - the caller would just see the same error reported twice

choices: The caller would stop receiving rejections from syncs that had failed
Concurrent syncs would start running in parallel instead of one at a time
After one failure, each later sync() chains onto a rejection and never runs
Nothing important - the caller would just see the same error reported twice

items.explanation: After one failed attempt every later sync() would chain onto a rejected promise, runOnce would never run, and syncing would silently stop until restart. Catching only on the internal tail keeps the queue alive while the caller still observes the failure.

items.prompt: A push returns 401 after the user has already logged out. What does runOnce do?

choices.text: It refreshes the token and retries the push, then quietly discards the new result
It returns at the generation check, without refreshing the abandoned account
It clears the outbox, because the session it belonged to is gone
It rethrows the 401 to the caller as an ordinary sync failure

choices: It refreshes the token and retries the push, then quietly discards the new result
It returns at the generation check, without refreshing the abandoned account
It clears the outbox, because the session it belonged to is gone
It rethrows the 401 to the caller as an ordinary sync failure

items.explanation: The generation check before refresh fails, so it returns without requesting new credentials. Checking before refresh (line 91) and after refresh (line 93) keeps a late 401 from restoring a logged-out session.

items.prompt: Why can the intersection at sync.ts:100-101 never filter anything in production today?

choices.text: The production adapter builds acknowledgedIds from the sent events themselves
Because runOnce skips the filter whenever the push succeeds on its first try
Because the outbox is cleared before each push, so no stale ids remain in it
Because TypeScript prevents ids outside the batch from reaching the filter

choices: The production adapter builds acknowledgedIds from the sent events themselves
Because runOnce skips the filter whenever the push succeeds on its first try
Because the outbox is cleared before each push, so no stale ids remain in it
Because TypeScript prevents ids outside the batch from reaching the filter

items.explanation: The push adapter maps acknowledgedIds from the sent events, so nothing outside the batch can arrive. It is belt-and-braces for a future adapter that trusts a server-supplied id list; keep it and pin it with a test.

items.prompt: The outbox holds 1,200 events when a sync starts. What does one runOnce send?

choices.text: The first 500 events, via readOutbox().slice(0, 500)
Pages of 500 until the outbox is empty, in one runOnce
The events recorded since the last successful sync
The 1,200 events together in a single push request

choices: The first 500 events, via readOutbox().slice(0, 500)
Pages of 500 until the outbox is empty, in one runOnce
The events recorded since the last successful sync
The 1,200 events together in a single push request

items.explanation: Each attempt reads at most five hundred outbox events; the rest wait for a later sync.

items.prompt: A profile update (updateMe) returns after a token refresh happened mid-flight. How does applyUserUpdate avoid restoring the outdated access token?

choices.text: It merges the returned user into the current tokens, not the captured ones
It replaces the token set with the one captured when updateMe started
It refreshes the token a second time before saving the updated profile
It drops the returned profile update whenever a token refresh happened mid-flight

choices: It merges the returned user into the current tokens, not the captured ones
It replaces the token set with the one captured when updateMe started
It refreshes the token a second time before saving the updated profile
It drops the returned profile update whenever a token refresh happened mid-flight

items.explanation: After the generation and account checks, { ...this.tokens, user } preserves newer credentials instead of rebuilding authentication from an old closure.
